summary.text: 鸡 is the common simplified form used for “chicken.” Its traditional graph 雞 is understood as an early bird picture that later appears in compound forms with a bird element and 奚 as a sound element. The first reported oracle-bone use is a place name, so the picture’s original referent is not certain.

formation.text: The historical graph 雞 is phonosemantic: 隹 or 鳥 supplies the bird category, while 奚 supplies a sound cue. Early forms are also interpreted as a whole chicken picture. The evidence supports these analyses but not a fully dated sequence from picture to compound. The modern shape 鸡 does not show a historical 又 + 鸟 construction.

components.text: Early forms of 雞 are interpreted as a whole picture of a chicken, with the crest and open beak emphasized. The earliest reported oracle-bone use is a place name, so the picture’s original referent is uncertain.

In 雞, 奚 supplies sound rather than its separate lexical meaning. Its Middle Chinese reading shares a rhyme with 雞 but has a different initial; the Old Chinese comparison is approximate and comes from a local cross-check.

sound_limitation.text: The exact Old Chinese forms in the local cross-check were not verified at the dataset publisher. 奚’s sound role in 雞 is stated explicitly in the historical dictionary account.

sound.text: The supplied Middle Chinese forms share a rhyme but differ in initial; modern Mandarin xī and jī also differ. The Old Chinese comparison is approximate.
sound.system: Middle Chinese categories and modern Mandarin; the Baxter–Sagart Old Chinese comparison *[g]ˤe vs *kˤe is approximate and based on a local cross-check

components.text: 隹 contributes the bird category in Qin and later forms of 雞. Some Warring States Qi and Chu forms use 鳥 instead; the evidence does not establish a single sequence between the two bird elements.

鳮 is recorded as a simplified-style variant associated with 雞 and appears as 鳮（雞） in the 1956 simplification scheme. The precise graphic route from that form to 鸡 is not documented; 又 has no supported historical role in 鸡.

history.text: The selected oracle-script image is a modern redraw of a form interpreted as a chicken picture, not an ancient inscription. The earliest reported oracle-bone use is a place name. One account says 奚 was later added as a sound marker because the picture could be confused with other birds, but the sequence is not fully dated.

The bird element varies across forms: some Warring States Qi and Chu forms use 鳥, while Qin and later forms use 隹. 鷄 is described as a Zhou-script form written with 鳥 and is treated as a graphic variant of 雞; the evidence does not establish a single linear path between them.
The 1956 simplification scheme lists 鳮（雞） and simplifies 鳥 as 鸟. It does not document the precise graphic route to 鸡 or support analyzing 鸡 as a historical 又 + 鸟 compound.

uncertainties.text: Early 雞 is interpreted as a chicken picture, but the earliest reported oracle-bone use is a place name. The picture’s original referent and earliest lexical meaning, and the timing of any transition to a compound, remain uncertain.
The bird element appears as both 鳥 and 隹 in different script traditions and periods. The evidence does not establish a complete sequence or show that 鳥 was only a later replacement.
The simplification evidence associates 鳮 with 雞 and lists 鳮（雞） but does not document the precise graphic steps to standardized 鸡.

senses.text: A Qin bamboo-slip passage is reported to use 雞 for chicken. The oracle-bone place-name use does not show whether this was the graph’s earliest animal meaning.

senses.period: oracle-bone script tradition; exact dating unresolved
senses.text: An oracle-bone use of 雞 is reported as a place name. This shows a use of the graph but does not establish the place-name’s referent or the graph’s original lexical meaning.

senses.gloss: 谿, valley or stream, written with 雞
senses.period: Mawangdui manuscript witness; exact borrowing date unresolved
senses.text: In a Mawangdui text, 雞 is reported as a phonetic loan for 谿, “valley” or “stream”; another manuscript copy has 溪. The graph was reused to write a different word, rather than “chicken” developing into “valley.” No contemporary pronunciations are supplied to demonstrate the proposed sound match.
The common current meaning is chicken.

limitations.text: The reported oracle-bone place-name use and Qin-slip animal use do not establish a direct semantic transition between them or identify the picture’s earliest lexical value.
The reported Mawangdui loan lacks contemporary pronunciations and a demonstrated sound rationale; its motivation and timing remain unresolved.

overview.text: 鸡 means “chicken.” Its traditional graph 雞 is interpreted as an early chicken picture, with later forms analyzed as a compound containing a bird element and sound-bearing 奚. The earliest reported oracle-bone use is a place name, so the original referent is uncertain.

components.text: Early forms of 雞 are interpreted as a whole chicken picture, though the earliest reported use is a place name and the picture’s original referent is uncertain.
奚 supplies sound in 雞, not its separate meaning. The Middle Chinese comparison shares a rhyme but differs in initial; the Old Chinese comparison is approximate.
隹 supplies the bird category in Qin and later forms. Other traditions use 鳥, so the written bird element varies.
鳮 is associated with 雞 and listed as 鳮（雞） in the simplification scheme; the precise route from it to 鸡 is not documented.

takeaway.text: The evidence does not establish 鸡 as a historical 又 + 鸟 compound; the visible shape alone cannot show that origin.

relationships.text: In the historical compound 雞, 奚 is explicitly identified as the sound-bearing element; this role belongs to 雞, not simplified 鸡.
